section_summary: This section contains diplomatic despatches from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo and internal memoranda from the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs spanning 1938 to 1941. It encompasses the final pages and communication schedules of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for April 1938, the full monthly report (No. 140) for May 1938 with associated despatch and telegram lists, and the initial pages of the report (No. 141) for June 1938. In addition, two Far Eastern Affairs division memoranda review Embassy reporting on Sino-Japanese and European relations for December 1938 and clarify the identity of the reactionary Japanese anti-Soviet society Meinkokukai.

subfiles.about: Concluding portion of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on political, military, and economic conditions in Japan during April 1938, with communication schedules.
subfiles.summary: Concludes the Embassy's review of Japanese affairs for April 1938, discussing press criticisms of Premier Konoe, War Minister Sugiyama's call for full national mobilization, and naval reassignments. It examines Minseito party leader Machida's calls for national unity and Home Minister Suetsugu's comments regarding a proposed new nationalistic political party following an earlier occupation of party headquarters by anti-communist activists. Economic reporting details trade deficits, import restrictions on wood pulp and rock phosphate, industrial recovery in Central China, and shipping fleet expansions, followed by complete lists of Embassy despatches (Nos. 2862–2910) and telegrams (Nos. 218–285) sent during April 1938.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of April, 1938 (Report No. 139)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing the Tokyo Embassy's monthly political and economic report for December 1938.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury provides an internal division critique and summary of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for December 1938. He notes that the summaries of Ambassador Grew's conferences with Foreign Minister Arita regarding American rights in China—including a tally of 296 incidents of injury to American property—and Ambassador Craigie's discussions offer no new information beyond previous reports. The memorandum also highlights report items noting the inauguration of a Japan-Peru Society in Tokyo on December 20 and an anticipated Japanese-German medical agreement.
subfiles.title: Tokyo's Monthly Report for December 1938

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting comprehensive Report No. 140 on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during May 1938.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Transmits Report No. 140 detailing major political and military events during May 1938. International relations sections report American protests over repeated aerial bombings of mission properties in China, the exclusion of Americans from occupied areas, and the British-Japanese agreement on the servicing of foreign obligations from Chinese Maritime Customs revenues. Military affairs cover the capture of Hsuchow, the naval occupation of Amoy, air operations over Hankow and Canton, and the formation of local collaborationist regimes. Major domestic developments include a significant Cabinet reconstruction bringing in General Ugaki as Foreign Minister, Seishin Ikeda as Finance/Commerce Minister, and General Araki as Education Minister, accompanied by lists of despatches (Nos. 2911–2964) and telegrams (Nos. 286–345) sent during May.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3029, Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of May, 1938 (Report No. 140)

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum identifying the Japanese reactionary anti-Soviet organization Meinkokukai.
subfiles.from: Frank A. Schuler, Jr., Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Responding to Under Secretary Sumner Welles following inquiries by the French Ambassador, Schuler clarifies that the organization reported as 'Bokokukai' is unknown under that name, but identifies it as the 'Meinkokukai'. The memorandum notes that the Meinkokukai is an ultra-nationalist group long prominent in Japan's anti-Soviet movement that has repeatedly agitated for war against the Soviet Union. Schuler references Tokyo Embassy's June 1938 political report, which noted the organization's distribution and posting of anti-Soviet handbills across Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for Mr. Welles on the Meinkokukai
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 141 on Japanese domestic and international conditions during June 1938 (initial pages).
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits Report No. 141 reviewing political, military, and international affairs for June 1938, containing the cover despatch, table of contents, and the first four pages of Section I. The text details extensive American diplomatic representations, including protests against the wounding of missionary Dr. Frederick G. Scovel by a Japanese soldier at Tsining, protests against assaults on Chinese crews of American launches in Shanghai, and Ambassador Grew's personal appeals against aerial bombing of Chinese civilian populations. It also records Japanese commitments regarding the restoration of the University of Shanghai and notifications by Minister-at-Large Tani restricting foreign shipping on the Yangtze River between Wuhu and Hukow.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3094, Transmitting Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of June, 1938 (Report No. 141)
